ii Offline Feedback Utilization for a Manual Aiming Movement Performed Under Conditions of Randomized Visual Feedback Availability Darian Cheng Master of Science in Exercise Sciences Graduate Department of Exercise Sciences University of Toronto 2009 Abstract Two studies were devised to determine why the difference in manual aiming performance, between full vision and no vision, is decreased for a randomized visual feedback schedule. In study one, aiming accuracy and precision was assessed for up to four trials in the same vision condition, following a switch in visual feedback availability. In experiment one, visual feedback availability was uncertain; while in experiment two, certainty was provided. Results of both experiments revealed that the precision of the first trial immediately following the switch in visual condition was reminiscent of the trial that preceded it, even when performed under different visual conditions. For study two, the inter-trial interval was evaluated by extending the interval to five seconds. Results indicated no reminiscence effect. Overall, we suggest that when the inter-trial trial is brief, individuals rely on offline visual information from the preceding trial to plan the subsequent movement, regardless of certainty.

1 1 General Introduction From pointing to a landmark in space to reaching for an object, our ability to perform goal-directed manual aiming tasks requires complex processing of sensory information. Generally, the dominant source of information that is used towards limb movements is visual information. This fact is highlighted by our inability to accurately reach for a target while in the dark as compared to when the lights are on (e.g., Carlton, 1992; Woodworth, 1899). As a result of our dependence on visual information, for accurate and precise movements, we have a highly evolved visual system to handle the different aspects of the visual stimuli (see Kandel, Schwartz & Jessell, 2000 for an overview). Another source of information that is used during limb movements is proprioception. As defined by Sherrington (1906), proprioception is the awareness of limb position and orientation indicated by receptors located in the muscles. Proprioceptive information is first gathered through specialized receptors located in different parts of the reaching limb. Specifically, receptors that are important to an aiming movement include muscle spindles, which are located in the muscle and provide information about muscle length and rate of change of muscle length. Muscle load information is provided by the Golgi tendon organs, which are located in the tendons of the muscles. Lastly, tactile sense is facilitated by tactile receptors, located at varying depths of the skin. As a result, there is a vast amount of information that is retrieved about the limb, which allows individuals to successfully keep track of its trajectory during manual reaches. 2 Review of Literature This review of literature covers the general models of limb control for manual reaching, from the use of sensory information prior to movement initiation, to its use during the movement. As well, the methodologies for examining sensory information utilization will be covered. 2.1 Models of Limb Control It was first suggested by Woodworth (1899) that aiming movements are characterized by two phases. The first phase, called the ballistic phase, is when the limb is propelled to the vicinity of the target location. This aspect of the limb movement is planned from visual information prior to movement initiation. While in the second phase, known as the current

<!-- Page 11 -->

2 control phase , the limb homes-in and lands on, or close to, the target. During this phase amendments to the limb trajectory occur, as evidenced by discontinuities of the limb trajectory. From Woodworth’s seminal model of rapid manual aiming, much iteration of the control models have been forwarded to explain the relative contribution between movement preplanning and online feedback during manual aiming. 2.1.1 Open Loop Control An open loop model suggests that the entire limb movement is planned in advance of its execution (Plamondon & Alimi, 1997). This includes not only the planning of the initial movement towards the target, but also the subsequent trajectory amendments, in the later stages of the movement. The information that is used to plan the movement is from prior experiences, which may include the outcome of the preceding trial(s). From this information, the relative contribution between the agonist and antagonist muscle of the effector limb is adjusted in order to reach the specified movement endpoint (Plamondon & Alimi, 1997). Support for the open loop model is provided by research from Bernier, Chua, Franks and Khan (2006), who found that, even though aiming movements performed with full vision (FV) were more accurate than aiming movements with no vision (NV), there was no difference in error reduction across both visual conditions. Specifically, when correlating the limb position at peak velocity versus movement end, the correlations were not different for both vision conditions, suggesting that participants did not make more movement corrections to the limb for FV than for NV. These correlations were made based on the assumption that low correlations indicate amendments were made to the limb trajectory, while high correlations suggest less limb correction (see also Heath, 2005; Messier & Kalaska, 1999). As a result, the authors posited that the advantage of FV trials over NV trials stemmed from the availability of visual information from the preceding FV trial, in particular information about the anticipated path of the limb as well as movement endpoint. A limitation to an entirely open loop model occurs when a perturbation is presented to the limb or environment – the model would predict that the limb should not be able to compensate for the perturbation. However this seems to not be the case, as perturbations incurred by the limb and/or the target during the course of the movement, are rectified if visual feedback is available (Elliott, Binsted & Heath, 1999). The ability to make online corrections during an aiming movement is advantageous because the location of a target(s) is not always fixed. From an

<!-- Page 12 -->

3 evolutionary standpoint, our visual system may have been developed to seek and hunt prey, which, as we know, are not necessarily targets that remain stationary. As a result, humans may have developed closed loop control in order to counteract the variability encountered while generating of the limb movement, and the variability of the target in the environment. 2.1.2 Closed Loop Control Closed-loop models have been forwarded to suggest how participants utilize visual information about the limb and target location to correct the trajectory of the limb during an aiming movement (see Elliott, Helsen & Chua, 2001 for a review). The Iterative Model proposed by Crossman and Goodeve (1983) suggested that an aiming movement is composed of a series of submovements, each containing a ballistic and current control phase (note: the study was presented at the Experimental Psychology Society meeting in 1963). Furthermore, each submovement is constant in time, but varies in terms of the distance the limb is from the target. Specifically, during the first submovement a large amount of error is expected to be encountered, because the limb is far from the target. However, on subsequent submovements, the amount of error would decrease because the distance from the limb to the target becomes shorter. Keele (1968) elaborated on this model, suggesting that each submovement covers a constant proportion of movement distance (i.e., around 1/7 of the distance between present location of the limb relative to the target). The limitation of this model was its inability to account for visual processing time. As visual processing has been estimated to be only as low as 100 ms (Carlton, 1992), it would not be possible for individuals for to use feedback in so many instances (i.e., 6-7 times) during an aiming movement. Another model proposed by Beggs and Howarth (1972) is the Single Correction model, where visual information about the limb and target environment is retrieved at an optimal time during the movement and used towards a single correction to the limb trajectory. It has been suggested that the optimal time for the retrieval of visual information may coincide with peak velocity, while the corresponding corrections occur during peak deceleration of the limb trajectory (Chua & Elliott, 1993). Furthermore, the Stochastic Optimized Submovement model proposed by Meyer, Abrams, Kornblum and Wright (1988) suggests that up to several corrections can be made during a limb movement, which depends on the variability of the initial movement towards the target. The variability in the initial movement towards the target is due to neuromotor noise, which may occur more often for movements of higher difficulty (i.e., large movement amplitude and/or small targets), therefore necessitating more

<!-- Page 13 -->

4 movement corrections. More recently, a Pseudocontinuous model, forwarded by Elliott, Carson, Goodman and Chua (1991) suggests visual information and trajectory corrections occur throughout the movement. Furthermore, these corrections do not necessarily result in discrete changes in the limb trajectory as assumed by earlier closed loop models. These assumptions were based on the fact that despite greater accuracy of FV trials over NV trials, there was no difference in discontinuities of the limb trajectories between vision conditions but greater time after peak velocity for the full vision condition (Elliott, Binsted & Heath, 1999). As a result, even within closed loop theories there is much debate as to how and when visual feedback is used during a limb movement. 2.2 Manipulation of Visual Feedback In the earliest research examining visual feedback utilization, experimenters manipulated vision by shutting off the lights in the examination room prior to or during the initiation of a limb movement (e.g., Keele & Posner, 1968). Using this method, all types of visual information (i.e., limb, target & environment) were removed. Other research methods have sought to isolate visual information of only the target or the limb, with the use of luminescent markers (e.g., Carlton, 1981). However, withdrawing vision has its limitations; as Weiss (1941) suggested, under circumstances of sensory information withdrawal, termed defect , the utilization of the remaining sources of sensory information will have changed. On the other hand, Weiss (1941) suggested transforming the sensory information of interest rather than over removing it. This type of method perturbs the modality of interest while not disrupting the utilization of other sources of information. Recent research methods have adopted this approach, by utilizing optical prisms to displace the visual field of the participant during aiming movements (e.g., Hansen, Elliott & Tremblay, 2008). Furthermore, with the advent of computer assisted experiments, experimenters have been able to manipulate the time course with which vision is available during a movement (Khan, Lawrence & Buckholz, 2004), as well as delaying the time with which the feedback is provided following movement end (e.g., Bernier et al., 2006). However it can be argued that occlusion methods are still evocative of what occurs with everyday life. 2.3 Certainty of Visual Feedback Availability As shown earlier, visual feedback has been manipulated in many ways in order to determine its contribution to the control of limb movements. One such factor that must be taken

<!-- Page 14 -->

5 into account while examining how individuals use visual information is the certainty with which visual feedback is be provided, from trial-to-trial during an experiment. In past research, visual feedback has often been manipulated in blocks of trials, that is, where a series of trials are all performed with visual feedback or without (e.g., Bernier et al., 2006; Zelaznik, 1983). This type of schedule presents the same visual information on every trial in the same block and provides participants with absolute certainty of visual feedback availability. Another type of scheduling is an alternating schedule, where vision and no vision trials are alternated from trial-to-trial (e.g., Khan et al., 2002). This form of scheduling provides different visual information on each trial, but still maintains a level of certainty of the visual feedback availability. Lastly, there is a randomized schedule, where visual feedback is randomly occluded from trial-to-trial (e.g., Elliott & Allard, 1985). As a result, not only does visual feedback have the possibility of varying from trial-to-trial, but unlike the first two types of schedules (i.e., blocked and alternating), random scheduling results in a high level of visual feedback uncertainty. The implication of the randomized visual feedback schedule has been examined by Elliott & Allard (1985). In the study, which was composed of three experiments, participants aimed at targets in the sagittal plane. In the first experiment, visual feedback was manipulated in blocks, while in the second experiment visual feedback was randomized from trial-to-trial. As expected, for the blocked protocol, participants were more accurate when they were aiming with vision of the limb and target, as compared to without. However, when vision was randomized on every trial, the difference in accuracy between full vision and no vision was not significantly different. As a result, due to the certainty provided by the schedule of visual feedback availability, individuals may adopt certain strategies to optimally cope with the availability, or lack of feedback, experienced throughout the block of trials. 2.4 Strategy vs. Preceding trial When availability of visual feedback is uncertain, participants may adopt strategies to optimize the use of the information available to them, however limited it may be. Elliott, Hansen, Mendoza and Tremblay (2004) suggested that when visual feedback is uncertain participants adopt a strategy where they plan for the worst-case scenario (i.e., no-vision). Specifically, as participants expect not to have vision on a large portion of trials in the experiment, they will rely more on movement planning rather than online visual feedback to control their movements.

<!-- Page 15 -->

6 Evidence for this ‘worst-case scenario’ also comes from Hansen, Glazebrook, Anson, Weeks and Elliott (2006). In the study, the certainty of the target location and visual feedback availability was manipulated in advance of every trial. The level of certainty of the visual condition and the target location varied depending on a precue, ranging from a single target to two targets (i.e., flashing of one or both placeholders where the target could be presented); and full vision or no vision or equal chance of both (i.e., placeholder would turn green, red or yellow). Results of the experiment showed that, when participants were aware of the target location and vision condition on each trial (e.g., single target with visual feedback certainty) participants were faster to react to the target and exhibited a longer movement time (i.e., associated with an increase time after peak velocity) for FV trials than NV trials. Longer movement times indicate that participants were using online visual feedback to amend the limb trajectory (e.g., Chua & Elliott, 1993). While when vision was uncertain, participants planned for the worst-case scenario, as their movement trajectories (i.e., across vision conditions) exhibited symmetrical profiles from the home position to the target (i.e., maximum limb velocity reached at approximately 50% of the distance to target). It is generally accepted in the current literature that symmetrical movements are indicative of more open loop control, which are movements that contain no or little online corrections (e.g., Messier & Kalaska, 1999). From these results, the authors concluded that under uncertain visual feedback availability, participants indeed plan for the worst-case scenario, as demonstrated by the slower movement times exhibited in full vision trials, when visual feedback was uncertain versus certain, as well as the predictive trajectory of the full vision aiming movements despite being provided with visual information. On the other hand, a preceding trial explanation forwarded by de Lussanet, Smeets and Brenner (2002). In the study, participants were required to hit a moving virtual target (i.e., a spider) on a computer screen using a stylus. The protocol subjected participants to four types of perturbations presented in separate blocks of trials. One perturbation type involved varying the target speed. Another perturbation type was an unexpected target jump. Two other perturbation types involved constant or varying force applied on the stylus. The authors hypothesized that, if participants use a strategy to execute their movements, then during a switch from one block to another, the task history from the preceding block should influence the movements of the following block. However, if participants execute their movements solely based on the events of the preceding trial, there should not be any carryover of context from the preceding block (i.e.,

<!-- Page 16 -->

7 trial-by-trial vs. block-by-block effects). The results of the experiment supported the preceding trial hypothesis, as participants showed adaptations based upon the specific block of trials in the experiment (i.e., speed, jump, force) but did not experience any carryover context effects from the preceding block. More importantly, the movement trajectories showed differences depending on the variation of the target stimuli from the preceding trial. As a result, the authors concluded that task history does indeed affect the characteristics of goal directed reaches, however it is limited to the preceding trial. In relating these findings to studies examining visual feedback utilization, we hypothesize that the smaller differences between FV and NV trials—when using a randomized schedule—is attributed to the influence of the preceding trial on the planning and execution of subsequent trials. 2.5 Offline Visual Feedback If indeed the preceding trial argument explains the results for manual aiming under a randomized protocol, it should be natural to examine how the offline feedback from the preceding trial contributes to subsequent trials. In a study conducted by Zelaznik, Hawkins and Kisselburgh (1983), participants were required to perform rapid aiming movements to a target with a 10 cm movement amplitude. Vision was manipulated (full vision: FV; no vision, NV) either a) in blocks, b) randomly, or c) with alternating visual feedback. As expected, the results of the first protocol (i.e., blocked schedule) showed that aiming with FV is more accurate than with NV. However, in the second protocol (i.e., random schedule) the advantage of FV over NV was still significant, but the difference in error was much less as compared to the first experiment. Based on these results, the authors suggested that participants were relying on offline information, that is, information from the preceding trial to plan and execute the following trials. Hence when FV and NV are randomized, there is less of an advantage of having vision over no vision, as compared to when the vision conditions are manipulated as a function of the block of trials. In the third protocol the authors hypothesized that if movements were programmed only with offline visual feedback from the preceding trial, then during an alternating schedule of FV and NV trials, the NV trials should be more accurate than the FV trials. The reasoning behind this hypothesis is that NV trials benefit from the use of offline visual feedback from the

<!-- Page 17 -->

8 preceding FV trials. Conversely, the lack of offline visual feedback from the preceding NV trial will lead to poorer accuracy for FV trials. However, the results of the experiment indicated that FV trials were more accurate than the NV trials, despite having less offline visual information from the preceding trials. From this finding the authors concluded that visual feedback was used online during the FV trial to increase accuracy. However, in considering the author’s methodology, a confounding factor in the study could have been the level of certainty of visual feedback availability. Therefore, research that remains to be carried out is a trial-by-trial analysis that contrasts manual aiming in different vision conditions while maintaining the same level of offline processing as a randomized protocol. Once this is established, certainty should be provided only by auditory cues, which manipulate the effect of advanced knowledge (i.e., certainty) without changing any aspect of the methodology. 2.6 Memory Guided Reaching Another factor that should be taken into account, when information is used from trial-to- trial, is the representation of the target. Elliott and Madalena (1987) suggested that the location of a target and its environment can be stored as a representation in memory for a period of up to 2 s after the target has disappeared. In the experiment, participants performed manual aiming movements to targets located 25 and 35 cm from a home position, while also manipulating vision by either providing vision throughout the entire trial or turning off the room lights upon, or prior- to movement initiation. Specifically, for the lights off conditions they varied the delay between the extinguishing of the room lights and movement initiation with delays of 0, 2, 5 and 10 s. The results of the experiment indicated that for total error (Henry, 1975) in movement amplitude, the 0 s delay condition was not different from the full vision condition, while the 2, 5 and 10 s delay conditions performed significantly worse. This result led the authors to suggest that a representation of the environment is useful for the control of a movement is available within 2 s of the target offset. Furthermore, the authors suggested that iconic memory could mediate these effects (see Coltheart, 1980). Iconic memory was first termed by Neisser (1967), based upon initial research by Sperling (1960), who found that when participants were briefly exposed to a matrix of letters and reported the letters in the matrix after its offset, their ability to do so depended on the method

<!-- Page 18 -->

9 with which they had to recall the letters. Specifically, if they were to recall as many letters as they could (i.e., free recall), they could only successfully report 4 out of the 12 letters. While in another recall condition (i.e., partial report procedure) they reported one of the three rows of letters in the matrix based upon a tone presented after the offset of the matrix (e.g., high tone = top row; low tone = bottom). In this condition they generally reported 3 out of the 4 letters in the row. Because participants were cued to the row after the offset of the matrix, the authors posited that participants encoded more letters of matrix during its presentation than what they could recall. Specifically, they believed participants could store up to 9 letters in iconic memory. Subsequent research has tried to further explore the characteristics of iconic memory. For instance, it has been found that when a delay (of greater than 150 ms) is introduced between display offset and cueing of the row, the advantage of performing the partial report over the free recall decreases until the ability of participants to report the letters are the same for both procedures, at the 1 s delay (Sperling, 1960). An alternative view to the iconic memory idea is the visual processing hypothesis set forth by Di Lollo (1977), who found that the ability of individuals to report items in the visual display depended not on the display offset, but rather on the onset of the visual stimulus. Normally, it is believed that the decay of the memory representation of the visual stimulus occurs with the offset of the visual stimulus. However, he demonstrated that if the duration of the display goes longer than 120 ms, individuals are unable to report the visual stimuli in the visual field, even if the duration between the target offset and task of reporting the stimulus is brief. As a result, Di Lollo (1977) suggested that iconic memory should be viewed as consequence of neural processing rather than a store for sensory information. More recently, Elliott, Calvert, Jaeger and Jones (1990) explored whether iconic memory is involved in memory guided reaches. The authors designed three experiments to explore the visual representation of the target environment and its possible connection with iconic memory. In the first experiment, visual prisms were used to laterally displace the visual environment, including the target. Also, they varied the delay between the target offset and movement initiation to determine the effect of the erroneous visual representation on manual aiming over a time period. The authors expected that as the delay between target offset and movement initiation increased, individuals would exhibit less movement error because the erroneous visual representation will have decayed from memory. In the second experiment, a pattern mask was

<!-- Page 19 -->

10 deployed between the target offset and movement onset. The purpose for using a mask was to disrupt memory representation of the target rendering individuals unable to perform accurate memory guided reaches. Lastly, an adaptation of the partial report procedure was modified to the manual aiming movement along with a variable delay between target offset and movement onset (i.e., 0, 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1000 ms). Specifically, participants were shown three target locations and were cued to aim to one of the three target locations after their offset (i.e., no- precue). In another condition (i.e., precue condition), participants were informed of the target they would have to aim to in at the beginning of the trial, even before the targets were presented. It was expected that individuals could aim accurately to either one of the three target locations (i.e., no difference between precue condition and no-precue condition), as long as the delay between target offset and movement onset is brief (i.e., less than 400 ms). The results of the first experiment, with the displaced visual field, demonstrated that radial error decreased as a function of delay. This result revealed that the effect of the erroneous target on the aiming task decreased gradually rather than abruptly. If indeed an iconic memory representation was used, an abrupt decrease in error would be expected around 250 ms, followed by a plateau in error in subsequent delays; however this was not the case. In the second experiment, aiming movements performed under the visual mask condition exhibited greater radial error than aiming performed without the interference of the pattern mask. This finding lends support to the idea that iconic memory contributes to this memory representation of the target. In the third experiment, it was found that there was no difference in radial error between the no-precue and precue condition when the delay between target offset and movement onset was 0 ms. As the delay increased individuals exhibited greater error in the no-precue condition, and this trend continued until the longest delay of 1000 ms. The authors concluded that the memory representation of the target environment does indeed exhibit effects of decay, as individuals were less influenced by the target representation (i.e., experiment 1 and 3) when the delay between target offset and movement onset increased. However, contrary to the iconic memory literature, which predicts an abrupt increase in error approximately 250 ms after the offset of the visual stimulus followed by a plateau, the results in this study generally displayed a gradual increase in error that continued to increase until the maximum duration of 1000 ms. As a result, whether iconic memory facilitates memory guided reaching remains unclear.

<!-- Page 20 -->

11 More recently, Binsted, Rolheiser and Chua (2006) had participants perform reciprocal aiming movements between two targets, for a duration of 11 s. During this time period, they provided vision of the limb and target during the first 5 s, while removing vision of the targets for the final 6 s. The purpose for this research was to estimate the decay of the representation that facilitates memory guided reaching. The findings of the experiment revealed that during the first 5 s of the trial, aiming was accurate and stereotyped. However, once vision of the targets was removed, individuals exhibited an increase in error that remained steady for 3 s (i.e., 5 - 8 s) and subsequently increased in the final seconds of the trial (i.e., 8 - 11 s). The authors concluded that while visual information is crucial for accurate movements, as suggested by a real-time hypothesis (Westwood & Goodale, 2003), the plateau in endpoint variability following the disappearance of the targets, also support the idea of a memory representation of the target (Elliott & Madalena, 1987). Using the real-time hypothesis to explain these results, when vision of the limb is not available, individuals may rely on the perceptual representation of the environment to execute their limb movements. This idea stems from the perception-action hypothesis, which proposes that visual information used for visual perception versus action, is facilitated by different neural substrates in the brain (Milner & Goodale, 1995). Specifically, after visual information is gathered into the primary visual cortex in the brain (i.e., V1), the information is then diverted to two different areas of the brain, which are believed to support specific visual functions. One route called the dorsal stream is the pathway in which visual information travels from the V1 dorsally to the posterior parietal cortex. This stream helps direct an individual’s limb towards an object during a goal-directed limb movement, providing information to individuals about their limb position and absolute size of the object they are reaching and/or grasping. However, research has indicated that this stream may only be in function when real-time information of the limb and the environment is available (Westwood & Goodale, 2003). As a consequence, when there is no vision of the limb during the movement, individuals will be unable to process information in this stream. The only information individuals can rely on is the perceptual representation of the object and environment in the ventral stream. Specifically, in this stream visual information travels from the V1 to the inferior temporal cortex. This stream serves the purpose of allowing individuals to perceive the environment by processing for colour, form and size contrasts between objects. In particular, as this stream relies on relative size contrasts between objects to process visual information, individuals are susceptible to size contrast illusions when making visual comparisons between

<!-- Page 21 -->

12 objects and when grasping for objects in size contrast illusions when vision is not available during the movement. In relating these assumptions to memory-guided reaching research by Binsted et al. (2006), the plateau in endpoint variability experienced after the visual information is removed can be explained by the real-time hypothesis. As during the reciprocal aiming, when vision is available individuals may be using the dorsal stream to process real-time visual information of the limb and target. However, when vision is removed, error increases slightly but plateaus for 3 seconds. This plateau may be experienced because individuals are relying on the perceptual representation from the ventral stream to continue guiding their movement. Therefore, although individuals do perform worse because they cannot rely on the dorsal stream to guide their movements, the perceptual representation from the ventral stream may be enough to facilitate their movements for up to a few seconds after the visual stimuli have been removed. 2.7 Study 1 Randomizing Visual Feedback in Manual Aiming: Reminiscence of the Previous Trial Condition and Prior Knowledge of Feedback Availability In this study, the trials following a switch in visual condition were examined for up to a maximum of four trials. Participants performed manual aiming movements to a single target while vision was provided or occluded, based upon eight trial sequences. In the first experiment participants were uncertain of the upcoming visual condition on each trial, and were exposed to a pseudo-random visual feedback schedule (i.e., actual 53% vs. 47% likelihood of changing vision condition or staying the same on the next trial, respectively). In the second experiment, a prerecorded voice presented prior to each trial provided visual feedback certainty. Based upon the previous research examining randomized visual feedback, under conditions of uncertain visual feedback (i.e., experiment one) individuals may adopt an overarching ‘worst-case scenario’ strategy where they plan to not have vision (Elliott, Hansen, Mendoza & Tremblay, 2004). On the other hand, when visual feedback is made certain by providing information about the availability of feedback before each trial, individuals should be able to use visual feedback to their advantage for the aiming movements performed in full vision (e.g., Khan et al., 2002). Another explanation is the preceding trial explanation, whereby individuals plan their movements based upon the availability of sensory information from the preceding trial (de

<!-- Page 22 -->

13 Lussanet et al., 2002). If this explanation is correct, then trials immediately following a switch in visual condition should exhibit the same levels of endpoint accuracy and precision as the trial that preceded it in the opposite visual condition. Furthermore, providing certainty or not prior to each trial should not make a difference in the outcome of both experiments. 2.8 Study 2 Does the Inter-trial Interval Facilitate the Use of Offline Information? For this second study, the importance of the inter-trial interval was examined by extending the inter-trial interval from 2.5 s (as found in study one) to 5 s during a uncertain visual feedback protocol. Based upon memory guided aiming research (e.g., Binsted, Rolheiser & Chua, 2006; Elliott & Madelena, 1987) it is believed that information about the target and its location can be used towards an aiming movement for a period of up to 2-3 s after the disappearance of the target. If indeed it is this same representation that facilitates the information from the preceding trial, then extending the inter-trial interval to beyond its limit should negate any effect of offline information from the preceding trial.

19 Offline Feedback Utilization for a Manual Aiming Movement Performed Under Conditions of Randomized Visual Feedback Availability Darian Cheng, Marlene Luis and Luc Tremblay Graduate Department of Exercise Sciences University of Toronto 2008 Abstract A trial-by-trial analysis was used to systematically examine the influence of switching visual conditions on visual feedback utilization for a manual aiming movement. In experiment one, vision was randomly manipulated from trial-to-trial with no more than four consecutive trials in the same visual condition. In experiment two certainty of visual feedback availability was provided prior to every trial. Results of both studies revealed that movement endpoint variability was most associated with visual feedback availability on the previous trial. Furthermore, a movment trajectory analysis revealed that the efficient of online corrections also depended on the availability of visual feedback on the previous trial. A second study revealed that these effects are These results suggest that the precision of an aiming movement is highly dependent on processing of offline visual information from the preceding trial.

<!-- Page 29 -->

20 Randomizing Visual Feedback in Manual Aiming: Reminiscence of the Previous Trial Condition and Prior Knowledge of Feedback Availability It is widely recognized that aiming movements performed with visual feedback are more accurate than those performed without (e.g., Keele and Posner 1968; Woodworth 1899). This is because individuals can employ the visual information to correct errors in the trajectory of the limb. Aiming movements are generally believed to be composed of two phases: an initial impulse phase , where the primary movement of the limb is made towards the target, and a current control phase, where visual feedback is used to correct the trajectory of the limb (Woodworth 1899). Many models of online control have been forwarded to explain the influence of the current control phase in the presence of visual feedback. For example, the single- correction model suggested by Beggs and Howarth (1972), proposes that visual feedback is used at an optimal time during movement execution, allowing for a correction to the limb trajectory to occur. In contrast, Meyer, Abrams, Kornblum, Wright and Smith (1988) demonstrated that several submovement corrections are made to the limb trajectory as it is homing-in on the target. Finally, Elliott, Carson, Goodman, and Chua (1991) forwarded the pseudo-continuous model, which suggests that visual feedback utilization is on-going throughout the entire duration of the movement. As a result, there are multiple interpretations describing visual feedback utilization during manual aiming that provide direct empirical support for closed-loop theories of limb control. Proponents of open-loop theories maintain that limb trajectories are preplanned prior to each movement. For example, Plamondon and Alimi (1997) suggested that amendments to the movement trajectory during a trial are actually based on information from previous trial(s). Research from Bernier, Chua, Franks and Khan (2006) lend some support to this theory, as they found that even though aiming in full vision (FV) was more accurate than in no vision (NV), there were no differences in the individuals’ ability to reduce variability (via corrections) across visual conditions. The authors suggested that the advantage of FV stemmed from offline visual information from preceding FV trials. Specifically, the visual information pertaining to the real-

<!-- Page 30 -->

21 time movement trajectory and endpoint position of the limb following a FV trial is used to plan the subsequent movement. However, this notion of feedforward control was previously challenged by Zelaznik, Hawkins and Kisselburgh (1983), who suggested that if the execution of rapid manual aiming was based entirely on offline visual information, then during an alternating pattern of FV and NV trials, the NV trials should be more accurate than the FV trials. This is because the NV trials would benefit from offline visual information from the preceding FV trial, while the FV trial would not benefit from the preceding NV trial. Indeed, when directly testing this hypothesis, FV trials remain more accurate than NV trials when presented in alternation (Khan, Elliott, Coull, Chua & Lyons 2002; Zelaznik et al. 1983). The above-mentioned research indicates several issues that should be considered when manipulating visual feedback availability during movement execution. Here we considered the number of trials in which there is a change/switch in vision condition, which encompasses the influence of visual feedback availability from the previous trials to the utilization of online visual feedback (i.e., during the current trial). Also, we considered the influence of strategy by providing prior knowledge of the upcoming vision condition. In this study, we systematically manipulated the number of trials within a vision condition (i.e., FV and NV) while scheduling a fixed number of switches between vision conditions. We analyzed the effect of trial order on feedback utilization following a switch in visual condition. That is, the accuracy and precision of each trial following a switch in visual conditions for up to four trials was examined, in order to determine the effect of offline and online visual information from trial-to-trial. Also, we manipulated prior knowledge of visual feedback availability to explore how participants may strategize the use of visual feedback. In experiment one, the random presentation order was unexpected by the participant. In the second experiment, participants were informed of the upcoming vision condition prior to each trial.

<!-- Page 31 -->

22 3.1 Experiment 1 The purpose of the first experiment was to examine the influence of visual feedback availability of a preceding trial on the utilization of visual information on upcoming trials during a randomized (i.e., uncertain) visual feedback protocol. If not knowing the upcoming vision condition leads participants to prepare for no vision at all (e.g., Elliott, Hansen, Mendoza & Tremblay 2004), there should be little or no differences in limb trajectories and movement endpoint distributions between FV and NV. Alternatively, if a limb trajectory exclusively relies on information from the preceding trial (e.g., Plamondon & Alimi 1997), these trajectories should be influenced more by the previous than the current vision condition. Therefore, we sought to determine if the performance of aiming movements during uncertain visual feedback conditions are a result of a strategy or a consequence of the preceding trial condition. 3.1.1 Methods 3.1.1.1 Participants Ten individuals (5 male, 5 female, mean age = 25 years, SD = 4.2) from the University of Toronto community participated in the study in exchange for a financial compensation of $5. All participants were right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were naïve to the purpose of the study. Informed consent was provided prior to the involvement in the experiment. Our research was approved by the University of Toronto Research Ethics Board and was therefore in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki. 3.1.1.2 Apparatus Participants were seated in a height adjustable chair in front of an aiming console located 84 cm above the ground. The console (52 cm x 30.5 cm) was constructed from translucent plexiglass and consisted of a home position (i.e., a 1 cm x 1cm textured tape) located 5 cm from the proximal edge. A single target, indicated by a light emitting diode (LED; 1 cm diameter) was mounted under the plexiglass surface of the board, 25 cm distal to the home position and was not visible unless it was activated. Also, two micro switches were mounted under home and target positions to detect movement start and movement end. Participants were fitted with a banjo pick equipped with an infrared emitting diode (IRED) which was monitored by an optoelectric tracking system at a sampling rate of 400 Hz (OptoTrak Certus, Northern Digital Inc.). Liquid

<!-- Page 32 -->

23 crystal goggles (Translucent Technologies Inc.) were used to manipulate visual feedback availability. 3.1.1.3 Design The experimental procedure consisted of 271 trials with 8 trial sequences. In four of the sequences, there was a FV trial followed by either: 1, 2, 3 or 4 trials in NV. For example, in one sequence there was a FV trial followed by one NV trial, while in another sequence there was a FV trial followed by four NV trials. The other four sequences were opposite, a NV trial followed by either: 1, 2, 3 or 4 trials in FV. As a result, there were forty 1 st trials, thirty 2 nd trials, twenty 3 rd trials, and ten 4 th trials in each vision condition. All sequences were presented randomly one after another with each sequence being performed ten times each. As a consequence, there were no more than four trials in the same visual condition. Also, the sequences were presented continuously such that the protocol was perceived as a long random series of FV and NV trials. 3.1.1.4 Procedure Each trial started with the goggles in the occluded state (i.e., translucent) with the participant’s index finger on the home position. When ready, the participant pressed down onto the home position, engaging the home position switch. At that point, the goggles turned transparent and the target was presented. After a 500 ms delay, a high pitched tone (800 Hz) indicated participants to aim as quickly and as accurately as possible to the target. For NV trials the goggles were occluded at movement initiation and for FV trials the goggles were occluded once the participant’s finger landed on the aiming surface, to limit terminal feedback. As a result, we solely manipulated information during movement execution. The participant was asked to keep his/her index finger at movement end until a low tone was presented (200 Hz), which indicated the end of the trial and instructed the participant to return to the home position for the next trial. 3.1.1.5 Data Reduction Displacement data was filtered using a second-order dual-pass Butterworth filter, with a cut-off frequency of 15 Hz (e.g., Heath, 2005). Instantaneous velocities were computed by differentiating displacement data with a three-point finite difference algorithm.

<!-- Page 33 -->

24 3.1.1.6 Dependent Measures and Analyses The dependent variables analyzed were movement time, time after peak velocity, as well as constant and variable error (i.e., CE, VE) in movement amplitude (Y-deviation) and direction (X-deviation). A 2 (vision: FV and NV) X 4 (successive trial: 1 st , 2 nd , 3 rd , 4 th in a sequence) repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted on all dependent variables. Finally, in order to determine if visual feedback availability influenced the presence of trajectory amendments, correlation coefficients (R) were calculated between final movement endpoint and 25%, 50%, and 75% of the movement trajectory for movement amplitude (Y-axis). These correlation coefficients were calculated in order to determine the extent to which limb trajectories were amended during movement execution (Heath 2005; Messier & Kalaska 1999). It has been suggested that when position at a portion of the movement highly predicts movement end (i.e., high correlation) the movement relies primarily on preprogramming. When the same comparisons lead to low correlations with movement end, it is understood that amendments are made to the limb trajectory as it unfolds. It is important to note that low correlations do not necessarily imply the use of sensory information during movement execution for the production of the amendments (see Plamondon & Alimi 1997) but higher correlations highlight more pre- planned movement trajectories. Further, the magnitude of the correlation coefficients only reflects the quantity of trajectory discontinuities and must be compared with endpoint accuracy and precision data to make inferences about their efficiency. In this study, we contrasted R using a 3 (proportion: 25%, 50%, 75%) X 2 (vision: FV and NV) X 4 (successive trial: 1 st , 2 nd , 3 rd , 4 th in a sequence) ANOVA. Post-hoc analysis of significant effects involving more than two means were performed using a Tukey HSD procedure with an alpha level set at .05 for all statistical tests. 3.1.2 Results There were no significant effects or interactions for movement time, F s < 1.0, p s > 0.4; time after peak velocity, F s < 1.1, p s > .3; constant error in movement amplitude, F s < 0.7, p s > .5; and constant error in movement direction, F s < 0.7, p s > .5. The analysis of variable error in movement direction revealed a main effect for vision, F( 1, 9) = 6.63, p < .05, and a main effect for trial, F (1, 9) = 3.05, p < .05. Variability in movement direction was significantly smaller in FV (0.79 mm) than in NV (1.02 mm) and participants were more variable on the 1 st trial than on a 4 th trial within a vision condition.

<!-- Page 34 -->

25 The analysis of variable error in movement amplitude revealed a main effect for vision, F (1, 9) = 26.8, p < .001, as well as a vision by successive trial interaction, F (3, 27) = 16.8, p < .001. Although variability in movement endpoint was significantly smaller in FV (4.85 mm) than in NV (6.22 mm), participants were actually less variable on the 1 st NV trial than on a 1 st FV trial (see Figure 1). Upon further examination of the vision by successive trial interaction, the first trial in any given condition was not different from the preceding trials in the opposite condition, and yet it was significantly different from the subsequent trials in the same condition. In terms of the relationship between limb position at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the movement versus limb position at movement end, there were main effects for movement proportion, F (2, 18) = 148.5, p < .001; and vision, F (1, 9) = 6.4, p < .05. Also, a significant two- way interaction was observed between vision condition and trial, F (3, 27) = 7.28, p < .001, in addition to a three way interaction involving all factors, F (6, 54) = 2.4, p < .05. The vision condition by trial interaction revealed that the correlation across all proportions of the movement and trajectory endpoint is: a) stable across the 2 nd , 3 rd and 4 th trials in FV, b) not different on the 1 st trial in a NV condition than in any FV trials, c) is significantly smaller in the 1 st trial in the NV condition than on the 3 rd and 4 th trial of the same condition, and d) is significantly smaller in the 2 nd trial in the FV condition than the 2 nd , 3 rd , and 4 th trial in NV. The breakdown of the three- way interaction (see Figure 2) revealed that: 1) FV yielded significantly stronger correlation coefficients than NV at 50% and 75% of the movement for the 1 st trial of a sequence; 2) FV yielded significantly weaker correlation coefficients than NV at: a) 25% of the movement for the 2 nd trial, b) 50% of the movement for all trials, and c) 75% of the movement for all trials ( p s < .05). Also, within vision condition comparisons of the same three-way interactions revealed significantly stronger correlation coefficients in the 2 nd , 3 rd and 4 th than in the 1 st trial for the 25%, 50% and 75% movement amplitude for the NV condition ( p s < .05). For the FV condition, weaker correlation coefficient were observed in the 2 nd than in the 1 st trial at 50% of the movement amplitude as well as in the 2 nd and 4 th than in the 1 st trial for the 75% movement amplitude ( p s < .05). 3.1.3 Discussion The analysis of variable error in movement amplitude revealed that, following a switch between vision conditions, the 1 st trial in a vision condition was not different from the 2 nd , 3 rd

<!-- Page 35 -->

26 and 4 th trial in the opposite vision condition. For instance if a sequence of FV trials were preceded by a NV trial, the 1 st FV trial would be just as variable as the NV trials. On the other hand, the opposite would occur if a sequence of NV trials were preceded by a FV trial. In addition, for any visual condition, variable error for the first trial in a vision condition was significantly different from the trials that followed, even though they were in the same vision condition. That is, it was not until the 2 nd trial with the same vision condition that the precision of the aiming movement became characteristic of the actual visual condition, with NV showing greater VE than FV and vice-versa. For variable error in movement direction a similar trend was found, however, differences were only yielded between the 1 st and 4 th trial within the same visual condition. The lack of differences between FV and NV across visual conditions for constant error in movement amplitude and direction is attributed to the large between subject variability in over and undershooting the target. As such, the constant error data followed the same pattern of results than the variable error data but did not reach conventional levels of significance. The correlation analyses between movement proportions (i.e., 25%, 50%, 75%) and movement end supported the findings mentioned above. Participants appeared to make significantly more amendments to their limb trajectory if they had vision on the previous trial. Specifically, the first trial in NV exhibited a low correlation, indicating amendments to the limb trajectory, which was not exhibited by the 2 nd , 3 rd and 4 th trials in NV for both 50% and 75% of the movement trajectory. On the other hand, the first FV trial exhibited a high correlation with movement end, indicating less movement amendments as compared to the 2 nd trial in FV during 50% of the trajectory and the 2 nd and 4 th trial for 75% of the movement trajectory, which attained higher correlations. As expected the correlations between 25% movement and endpoint did not yield as many differences between vision conditions as compared to 50% and 75% of the movement trajectory (see Heath 2005). Combined with the precision results, it appears that efficient online corrections of limb trajectories necessitate vision on the previous trial. As such, when subjected to a 1 st trial in NV, participants made amendments to their limb trajectory as the correlations with movement end were comparable and just as effective as the 2 nd , 3 rd5 , and 4 th trial in FV. A plausible explanation for this finding is that online corrections in the first NV trial were based on proprioception that was calibrated from the previous FV trials. On the other hand,

<!-- Page 36 -->

27 when presented with vision for the first time (i.e., 1 st FV trial), participants did not appear to make many online amendments to the limb, even though visual information was readily available. Using the offline explanation (i.e., Plamondon et al. 1997), it could be that individuals used visual information from the completed FV trial to program the next movement (e.g., Plamondon & Alimi 1997; see also Zelaznik et al. 1983). That is, whenever visual information was available on a trial (i.e., FV); it was used to plan the subsequent movement. In the absence of vision on the preceding trial (i.e., NV), there is no visual information to use towards programming the next movement (e.g., 1 st FV trial). Therefore, looking back at Elliott and Allard (1985), the smaller differences obtained between FV and NV trials for the randomized protocol—as compared to blocked vision protocol—can be explained by offline processing of information from the preceding trial. Indeed, we can expect poor performance on a 1 st trial in FV, due to the lack of offline visual processing from the preceding NV trial while the 1 st trial in NV benefits from offline visual information from the preceding FV trial. Furthermore, this use of offline information from the preceding trial may ultimately be a result of strategy adoption. Specifically, when vision is uncertain participants may plan for the ‘worst-case scenario’ (i.e., no vision on the next trial) and draw visual information from the next most reliable resource: The preceding trial. Thus, we deemed relevant to assess whether prior knowledge of the vision condition can influence this trial-by-trial effect of visual information utilization. 3.2 Experiment 2 The purpose of the second experiment was to determine if providing certainty of visual feedback availability before every trial affects its utilization in a randomized vision schedule. Specifically, can individuals take advantage of online visual feedback if they are told prior to a trial whether or not vision will be available? If individuals were preparing for the worst-case scenario (e.g., Elliott et al. 2004) in experiment one, then eliminating visual feedback uncertainty should reduce or void the influence on offline processing of visual information. Conversely, if participants were simply using visual information from the previous trial, then eliminating visual feedback uncertainty should lead to the same results as experiment one, with NV trials more precise than FV trials immediately following a switch in visual condition.

<!-- Page 37 -->

28 Available evidence for the use of certain versus uncertain visual feedback suggests that knowing the upcoming vision condition influences visual feedback utilization (Khan et al. 2002; Zelaznik et al. 1983). However, in both studies, visual feedback was alternated from trial-to-trial with auditory warnings of the upcoming visual condition. Thus, considering the results for the first trial in each vision condition, we believe it is relevant to assess whether knowing the upcoming vision condition is also advantageous when vision conditions are randomized. 3.2.1 Methods 3.2.1.1 Participants Twelve individuals (6 male, 6 female, mean age = 23 years, SD = 1.9) from the University of Toronto community participated in the study in exchange for financial compensation of $5. Participants were right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were naïve to the purpose of the study. Informed consent was provided prior to the involvement in the experiment. Our research was approved by the University of Toronto Research Ethics Board and was therefore in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the Declaration of Helsinki. 3.2.1.2 Design and Procedure The experimental design and procedures were the same as those used in experiment one, however participants were informed of the upcoming visual condition prior to each trial. Specifically, a recorded voice stating ‘full’ for a FV trial or ‘none’ for a NV trial was played by the custom E-Prime software prior to each trial. These procedures were executed while maintaining an inter-trial interval of 5 s for both experiments. 3.2.1.3 Data Reduction, Dependent Measures and Analyses The data reduction procedures, the dependent variables and the analyses were the same as in experiment one. 3.2.2 Results There were no significant effects or interactions for movement time, F s < 0.75, p s > .5; time after peak velocity, F s < .38, p s > .7, and constant error in movement amplitude F s < .35, p s > .7. For constant error in movement direction there was a main effect of vision, F (1, 11) =

<!-- Page 38 -->

29 7.7, p < .05, as aiming movements in FV were more to the right than in NV. Also there was a vision by successive trial interaction, F (3, 33) = 5.72, p < .01. However, as in the first experiment, the post-hoc analysis did not yield any significant differences between the relevant means. As opposed to the results of experiment one, variable error in movement direction, revealed no significant effects or interactions, F s < 1.24, p s > . 3. However, the results for variable error in movement amplitude of experiment one were replicated in experiment two. Specifically, there was a main effect of vision F (1, 11) = 31, p < .001 as FV trials exhibited less variability than the NV trials (4.7 mm and 5.8 mm error respectively). Also, there was a vision by successive trial interaction, F (3, 33) = 40, p < .001. The post hoc analysis revealed that participants were actually less variable on a 1 st NV trial than on a 1 st FV trial (see Figure 3). Also, the first trial in any vision condition was significantly different than the subsequent trials in the same vision condition. In terms of the correlation analyses between position at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the trajectory as compared to movement endpoint, there was a main effect of movement proportion, F (2, 22) = 254.7, p < .001, a significant interaction between vision and successive trial, F (3, 33) = 4.6, p < .01, and a three way interaction involving all factors, F (6, 66) = 7.8, p < .001. As expected, correlation coefficients increased significantly between each movement proportion ( p s < .001). Also, the vision by successive trial interaction revealed significantly larger correlation coefficients in the 4 th than in the 1 st trial for the NV but not for the FV condition. The breakdown of the three-way interaction (see Figure 4) revealed that: 1) FV yielded significantly stronger correlation coefficients than NV at 50% and 75% of the movement for the 1 st trial of a sequence; 2) FV yielded significantly weaker correlation coefficients than NV at: a) 25% of the movement for the 3 rd trial, b) 50% of the movement for the 4 th trial, and c) 75% of the movement for the 3 rd and 4 th trial ( p s < .05). Also, within vision condition comparisons of the same three-way interactions revealed significantly stronger correlation coefficients in the 3 rd and 4 th than in the 1 st trial for the 50% and 75% movement amplitude for the NV condition ( p s < .05). For the FV condition, weaker correlation coefficient were observed in the 3 rd than in the 1 st trial at 50% of the movement amplitude as well as in the 3 rd and 4 th than in the 1 st trial for the 75% movement amplitude ( p s < .05).

<!-- Page 39 -->

30 3.2.3 Discussion In experiment one, the results indicated that participants used information from the previous trial in order to plan the subsequent movement visual feedback was uncertain. In this experiment, visual feedback certainty was provided in order to determine if individuals can better prepare their movement or optimize their online use of proprioceptive information prior to an aiming movement. The results of this second experiment indicate that participants remained significantly dependent on visual information from the previous trial, even when informed of the upcoming visual condition. Particularly, on the 1 st FV trial, participants were still unable to benefit from the current visual information even though they were told they were going to receive it. This result seems to contradict the findings of Khan et al. (2002) and Zelaznik et al. (1983). However, the fact that we randomized the experimental conditions instead of alternating while providing advance information about the vision condition can explain the discrepancies between this study and those from other laboratories. The correlation analyses in the second experiment revealed a similar pattern of results as experiment one. Specifically, participants exhibited a stronger correlation between position at 75% of the trajectory and movement end for the 1 st as compared to the 3 rd and 4 th trial in FV. As such, even if they knew they would have vision, they made significantly fewer amendments to their limb trajectory when vision was presented for the first time in a sequence (i.e., preceding trial in NV). Therefore, when given knowledge that visual information will be available for the first time on the upcoming trial, participants appeared not to be able to use visual information for online control. Thus, knowing the upcoming vision condition is not sufficient to make appropriate use of it (e.g., reduce endpoint variability) 1 . 3.3 General Discussion First, there were many consistencies between the experiments. If participants were presented with the same vision condition twice in a row, they adjusted their limb trajectory in the latter portion of the movement significantly more when they had vision than when they did not. Secondly, the presence of corrections in the latter portions of the trajectory—as evidenced by lower correlation coefficients—were associated with endpoint precision measures (i.e., variable error in movement amplitude). Specifically, the presence of corrections after 75% of the trajectory was directly associated with a reduction in variable error of movement amplitude. For

<!-- Page 40 -->

31 instance, the distribution of movement endpoints (i.e., VE) was larger in the 1 st than the 2 nd , 3 rd , and 4 th trial in FV across experiments. Even though participants knew in advance they would be switched to FV (i.e., experiment two) they did not appear to try to use the online visual feedback. Further, in both experiments, participants made significantly more corrections on the 1 st than the 3 rd , and 4 th trial in NV and these corrections on the 1 st trial were effective enough to yield a lower variable error. Thus, our results can explain the discrepancy between predicted results predicted by closed-loop theories and studies manipulating advance information about visual feedback availability (i.e., strategy). Open-loop theories suggest that accuracy on any given trial primarily depends on visual information available from a preceding trial (e.g., Plamondon and Alimi, 1997). In such case, alternating between vision conditions from trial-to-trial (e.g., Zelaznik et al. 1983), should lead to more accurate movement endpoints in NV than in FV. Indeed, the trajectories performed in FV would be based on the previous NV trial and vice-versa. However, studies alternating vision condition did not find this result and nor did we, because FV was generally more precise than NV. However, when we looked at specific trials in a sequence it was found that vision on the preceding trial would lead to greater movement amendments during the trial and result in a precise movement, regardless of the current vision condition. While on the other hand if there was no visual information on the preceding trial, it would most often lead to less movement amendments and a larger distribution of movement endpoints. Most interestingly, when participants were presented with vision and were warned of it, they appeared to make fewer trajectory corrections if the previous trial was in NV than if it was in FV. The fact that participants did not make significant amendments on the 1 st FV trial does not support the idea that individuals were using a cognitive strategy. It has been previously suggested that uncertainty of visual feedback from trial-to-trial leads individuals to plan for the worst-case scenario (i.e., no vision) and place a greater emphasis on movement planning over online control (see Elliott et al. 2004). Such strategy would predict less of an advantage in performance of FV over NV in experiment one than in experiment two. However, this was not the case. Rather, overall differences between FV and NV were comparable between experiments. The observed importance of the previous trial has also been observed for other task types in which target displacement characteristics and movement constraints (e.g., de Lussanet, Smeets, Brenner 2002) as well as task difficulty (e.g., Song, Nakayama 2007) were explored 2 . Both

<!-- Page 41 -->

32 experiments in our study extend these observations to visual information utilization for manual aiming. Further, the additional trajectory analysis provides us with some extra insight. Results of both experiments showed that endpoint variability was directly associated with visual feedback availability on the previous trial, regardless if participants were told in advance of the upcoming visual condition. At the very least, our study allows for suggestion that models of on-line visual feedback utilization must consider visual information utilization from the previous trial. As such, information from the previous trial could either be used to generate a motor plan that is implemented in an open-loop fashion or employed to generate a sensorimotor representation that is compared with online information—perhaps proprioceptive—on the current trial. 3.4 Conclusion In this study, we considered the proportion of trials in which there is a change/switch in vision condition. In order to do so, we broke down this methodological factor into the influence of repetition (i.e., being presented with multiple trials of the same vision condition in a row) on the utilization of on-line feedback. Our observations of limb trajectory corrections and endpoint precision strongly suggest that participants relied on information available in the previous trial. As such, studies randomizing vision conditions should consider analyzing the first trial following a switch in vision condition separately from subsequent ones when vision availability is present on 50% of the trials. We also considered the influence of strategy by providing prior knowledge of the upcoming vision condition. As stated above, such advance information can change the strategy of the participant. However, our experiment failed to demonstrate that prior knowledge of the upcoming vision condition affects the way individuals use visual information. Finally, we conclude that visual information available on the previous trial could either be used to plan the upcoming movement’s trajectory amendments (e.g., Plamondon & Alimi 1997) or utilized to form a sensorimotor representation that would be available for the next trial (e.g., proprioceptive calibration function).
