40 The representation of offline information from the preceding aiming trials with an extended inter-trial interval Most research examining visual feedback utilization has shown that, when vision is available during aiming, the outcome of the movement will be more accurate than without vision (Carlton, 1992). This is presumably because the visual information is used as feedback to control the limb during the course of the movement (e.g., Elliott, Binsted & Heath, 1999; Woodworth, 1899). However, not all visual manipulations lead to clear differences in endpoint accuracy between movements performed with or without vision (i.e., full vision: FV vs. no vision: NV). Studies pertaining to visual feedback use, and manual aiming have often employed blocked protocols, wherein the same visual condition is administered on every trial in a block. This type of research highlights how the visual feedback is used under predictable circumstances. However, when visual feedback availability from trial-to-trial is made uncertain—by randomizing the visual conditions—the benefits of having vision during the aiming movement is reduced or even at times non existent (e.g., Elliott & Allard, 1985). One explanation that has been forwarded to explain the smaller difference of performance between FV and NV is strategy . It has been suggested that the smaller discrepancy in movement endpoint error found between FV and NV is attributable to an adoption of an overall strategy where participants plan for the worst-case scenario (i.e., NV: see Elliott, Hansen, Mendoza & Tremblay, 2004). As a result, participants may plan their movements in advance assuming vision will not be available on the upcoming trial. Consequently, even if vision is available, the individuals performing the aiming movement would not use it as efficiently as compared to a situation in which they expect to have visual feedback (Zelaznik et al, 1983). Such an explanation predicts that participants are more efficient at using visual information, when its availability is made certain, which would be reflected by longer movement times and asymmetric limb trajectories for the FV trials only (see Hansen et al., 2006). Another explanation for the smaller differences in performance between FV and NV under randomized protocols (i.e., compared to blocked) is that only trials immediately following a switch in vision conditions are affected by the previous trial. During a randomized protocol, several trials can be performed consecutively in a visual condition before the visual condition

<!-- Page 50 -->

41 must change on the next trial (e.g., Khan et al., 2002). Therefore, the performance of the first trial in FV following a NV trial may be hindered as compared to subsequent FV trials that may follow, while on the other hand a NV trial may benefit from having FV trials that precede it, performing better than subsequent trials in NV. These results are under the assumption that participants plan their movements based upon the availability of sensory information on the trial immediately preceding it (i.e., preceding trial hypothesis; deLussanet, Smeets & Brenner, 2002). Recently, Cheng, Luis & Tremblay (2008) examined the consequence of randomized visual feedback on manual aiming using a trial-by-trial analysis. Specifically, we wanted to examine the effect of the preceding vision condition (e.g., FV), on subsequent trials in the opposite vision condition (e.g., NV), for up to four trials. In order to do so, we systematically organized the experimental trials into eight trial sequences, which varied the number of trials following a switch in vision condition. Specifically, in one sequence there could be one FV trial followed by four NV trials (i.e., FV-NV4), or one NV trial followed by two FV trials (i.e., NV- FV2). Therefore, when presenting these sequences in a continuous manner the protocol seemed entirely randomized to the participant, while it allowed the experimenters to systematically examine the effect of the switch in vision condition on subsequent trial(s). The results of the experiment supported the preceding trial explanation (i.e., reminiscence effect) because the trials immediately following a switch in vision condition showed the same level of precision as the trials that preceded it. For example the first NV trial exhibited a low variable error much like the typical FV trial that preceded it (i.e., prior to the switch in vision condition)—while low endpoint precision was exhibited for the first FV trials. Furthermore, the same pattern of results was found in the trajectory amendment analyses: the first trial following a switch in vision condition showed the same level of trajectory variability as the trial preceding it (i.e., low correlation if preceded by FV trials and high correlation if preceded by NV trials). Also, this reminiscence effect was replicated in a second experiment in which the same protocol was used, except participants were told whether they would receive visual information in advance of each trial. However, advance knowledge of the vision condition did not significantly influence the observed reminiscence effect. This research supported the use of preceding trial information to plan subsequent movements. As well, the same study also provided some empirical evidence against the worst-case scenario hypothesis.

<!-- Page 51 -->

42 One major issue of concern in all of these studies—which is rarely considered—is the inter-trial interval used in the experimental method. In Cheng et al. (2008) a relatively brief inter- trial interval of 2.5 s was used, while the inter-trial interval is arbitrarily documented in most studies (Elliott & Allard, 1985; Hansen et al., 2006; Zelaznik et al., 1983). The length of the inter-trial interval may have a large implication for offline feedback utilization, especially when it goes beyond three seconds. This is because offline information from the preceding trial may be stored in a memory buffer. Based upon the influential paper by Elliott and Madelena (1987), visual feedback about target location is believed to be stored in memory for up to a period of 2 s. In the study, Elliott and Madelena (1987) had participants perform aiming movements to targets located 25 and 35 cm from a home position. There were two vision conditions: FV and NV. In the movements in NV there were four possible delays between the extinguishing of the room lights and the signal indicating to initiate the aiming movement (i.e., 0, 2, 5 & 10 s). The results of the experiment revealed that, when aiming to a target after a delay of less than 2 s, movement accuracy was not significantly different from FV, while 2 s and beyond, the endpoint accuracy was significantly worse. More recent research has also examined the idea of a memory representation of a target and its location during a repetitive aiming task (Binsted, Rolheiser & Chua, 2006). That is, instead of using a single discrete aiming movement, the authors made participants perform a reciprocal aiming task (i.e., Fitts’s task) in the transverse axis (30 cm amplitude). Each trial lasted 11 s, with the individuals performing the movement with vision of both the target and home position and the hand during the first 5 s. For the remaining 6 s of the trial, vision of the target was made unavailable. The results of the experiment revealed that, when vision was removed after the first 5 s of the trial, there was an increase in variable error, that is the distribution of endpoints was greater than aiming with vision of the target, but error remained the same for 3 s. For the remaining 4 s (8 - 11 s of the trial) variable error increased even further. From these results, the authors concluded that the accuracy of an aiming movement will decrease once vision is removed, which supports a real-time hypothesis, where it is believed that accurate control of a movement requires concurrent vision of the target. However, the plateau in variable error in the 3 s following the removal of the target also supports the work of Elliott and Madalena (1987) where memory of a target and its location can be used to control a movement.

<!-- Page 52 -->

43 Altogether, the present study we sought to determine if the reminiscence effect observed by Cheng et al. (2008) is attributable to offline information utilization stored in a memory representation. The purpose of this study was to determine if individuals are using offline information from the preceding trial to execute the following trial when the inter-trial interval is 5 s. It is expected that because the inter-trial interval is 5 s, all effects of the preceding trial should be negated. If this is the case, then perhaps participants will revert to the worst-case scenario and plan not to have vision, as participants will be uncertain of the availability of visual feedback on each trial. 4.1 Experiment 4.1.1 Methods 4.1.1.1 Participants Ten participants (4 male, 6 female, mean age = 21 yrs, SD = 3.4) completed the study in return for compensation of $5. Participants were recruited from the University of Toronto Community and were self-declared right-hand dominant with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. The experimental protocol was approved by the Research Ethics Board at the University of Toronto and was in compliance with the 1964 declaration of Helsinki. 4.1.1.2 Apparatus Aiming movements were performed on a plexi-glass aiming console. The home position was indicated by a piece of textured tape located on the proximal edge of the board. A single target position (1 cm in diameter) was indicated by a green light emitting diode mounted under the surface of the board. The target was not visible to the participants unless it was activated. The position of the index finger was tracked using an optoelectric motion tracking device, OptoTrak by Northern Digital Inc. Specifically, participants were fitted with a banjo pick on the index finger which contained an infrared emitting diode. The diode was tracked by infrared cameras at 400Hz. Visual feedback availability was manipulated using liquid crystal goggles (Translucent Technologies Inc.). All equipment was controlled using custom MatLab software (The Mathworks Inc.). Lastly, Participants were seated in a height adjustable chair set to their comfort level.

<!-- Page 53 -->

44 4.1.1.3 Design The experiment was composed of 271 trials. FV and NV trials were administered through 8 trial sequences. Specifically, in four of the sequences, one FV trial was followed by 1, 2, 3 or 4 NV trials. While for the four remaining sequences the opposite, that is: one NV trial followed by 1, 2, 3 or 4 FV trials. All sequences were randomly presented in a continuous manner and performed 10 times each. 4.1.1.4 Procedure Each trial started with the goggles in the occluded state and as a result participants were required to feel their way to the textured home position. The goggles were then triggered to become transparent and the target LED was activated, revealing its location. Following a 500 ms delay, a high-pitch tone (800 Hz) indicated the participants to aim as quickly and as accurately as possible to the target location. On trials without visual feedback, the goggles were occluded upon initiation of the movement, while for trials with visual feedback; the goggles were occluded once participants landed within the vicinity of the target. Participants were instructed to keep their index finger at the movement end until a low tone (200 Hz) indicated them to move back to the home position. The inter-trial interval was maintained between trials by not allowing the next trial to be initiated until 5 seconds elapsed after the end of the movement. 4.1.1.5 Data Reduction A three-point infinite difference algorithm was used to compute Instantaneous velocities from the limb displacement data. Movement start and movement end were identified when the velocity of the index finger rose above or fell below 300 mm/s, respectively. 4.1.1.6 Dependent Measures and Analysis Temporal measures used in the experiment were movement time, time after peak velocity. Spatial measures were constant and variable errors (i.e., CE, VE) in movement amplitude (Y-deviation) and direction (X-deviation). A 2 (vision: FV and NV) X 4 (successive trial: 1 st , 2 nd , 3 rd , 4 th in a sequence) repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted on all dependent variables. Also, to determine the presence of trajectory amendments in movement amplitude (Y-axis), an analysis of movement variance was conducted. The analysis consisted of squaring the correlation between the final movement endpoint with limb position at

<!-- Page 54 -->

45 25%, 50%, and 75% of the movement trajectory (Heath 2005; Messier & Kalaska 1999). It has been suggested that when position at a portion of the movement highly predicts movement end (i.e., high R 2 values) the movement relies primarily on preprogramming. When the same comparisons lead to low R 2 values with movement end, it is understood that amendments are made to the limb trajectory as it unfolds. It is important to note that low R 2 values do not necessarily imply the use of sensory information during movement execution for the production of the amendments (see Plamondon & Alimi 1997) but higher R 2 values highlight more pre- planned movement trajectories. Further, the magnitude of the R 2 values only reflects the quantity of trajectory discontinuities and must be compared with endpoint accuracy and precision data to make inferences about their efficiency. In this study, we contrasted R 2 using a 3 (proportion: 25%, 50%, 75%) X 2 (vision: FV and NV) X 4 (successive trial: 1 st , 2 nd , 3 rd , 4 th in a sequence) ANOVA. A Tukey HSD post-hoc analysis procedure with an alpha level set at .05 was performed on significant effects and interactions involving more than two means. 4.1.2 Results There were no significant effects for movement time, F < .88, p > .37; time after peak velocity F < .63, p > .45; constant error in movement direction, F < 1.41, p > .27; constant error in movement amplitude, F < 2.73, p > .063; variable error in movement direction, F < 1.64, p > .203. For variable error in movement amplitude, there was a main effect of vision F (1, 9) = 47.1, p < .001, as trials performed in FV were less variable than those performed in NV, with 5.24 mm and 8.21 mm variable error respectively. A vision by trial interaction for variable error, F (3, 27) = 6.36, p = .002, revealed that all FV trials were significantly less variable than all NV trials ( p s < .01). Also, within vision conditions there were no differences between FV trials ( p s > .52), but for the NV conditions, the 1 st trial was less variable than the 3 rd and 4 th ( p s < .01) (see Figure 5). The R 2 analysis of movement variance between the limb position at various movement time proportions and limb position at movement end revealed main effects for vision, F (1, 9) = 52.95, p < .01, and movement proportion, F (2, 18) = 72.66, p < .01. Also, there were two-way interactions involving vision and movement proportion, F (2, 18) = 71.81, p < .001; and movement proportion and trial order, F (6, 54) = 2.55, p < .05. Breaking down the vision by movement proportion interaction (see figure 6) revealed that at 25% of the movement there were no differences in R 2 values between FV and NV. However, at 50% and 75% of the movement,

<!-- Page 55 -->

46 NV yielded higher R 2 values than FV. Further, R 2 values increased across all movement proportions for NV but only between 50% and 75% of the movement for FV. The breakdown of the movement proportion by trial interaction (see figure 7) revealed that all trials at 25% and 50% movement proportion were not different except for the 1 st trial at 25% and 2 nd trial at 50%. While at 75% movement proportion, movement trajectories had higher R 2 values than those at 25% and 50% of movement proportion. 4.1.3 Discussion Overall, the results of the experiment reflect an expected main effect for vision as well as a novel observation of repeating the NV condition many trials in a row. The results of the experiment revealed that NV trials were less precise than FV trials (i.e., lower variable error in movement amplitude in FV than NV). This result was supported by the analyses of movement variance, as FV trials almost always attained a lower R 2 value with movement end than NV trials. In referring these results to a limb control perspective, it seems as though when individuals are performing aiming movements in FV, they are using closed loop control. This is because FV trials generally exhibited a lower R 2 value with movement end than NV trials across all movement proportions, indicating more corrections were made when vision was available. On the other hand, when aiming in NV, individuals attained a higher variable error as compared to FV trials, probably because they were not able to exploit the information from the preceding trial to execute their movements. However, this effect varied as a function of the number of subsequent trials in NV. Comparing this finding to that of study one, which revealed that when the inter-trial interval was brief (i.e., 2.5 s) the first trial in FV trial exhibited a high variable error and low correlation with movement end, compared to the first NV trial. It was suggested that individuals were simply using information from the previous trial to execute the upcoming trial, because having a NV trial preceding the first FV trial always compromised movement precision and the ability to perform online corrections. Also, the vision condition on the preceding trial may have been used as a cue for the subsequent trial. As a result, the second trial and beyond in FV exhibited higher precision scores along with lower correlations with movement end as compared to the first FV trial. However, these findings were not replicated in this experiment.

<!-- Page 56 -->

47 In fact, individuals appeared to be able to use visual information on the first trial that it was available, and this level of endpoint precision was maintained throughout subsequent trials in FV. We believe these results were obtained because with the longer inter-trial interval (i.e., 5 s), visual and proprioceptive information from preceding action may have decayed significantly from the memory systems. As a consequence, individuals may have treated each trial separately because of that lack of information from the preceding trial. There were differences in the variable error for movement amplitude as a function of the trial order for the NV condition; the 1 st trial in NV was less variable than the 3 rd and 4 th trial. Such influence effect of trial in NV on trajectory endpoint was in part reflected in the analyses of movement variance. Indeed, what is intriguing is that at 25% and 50% of the movement, the 4 th trial in NV had a tendency to yield lower R 2 value as compared to the other trials (i.e., 1 st , 2 nd and 3 rd trials). Two explanations can be forwarded to explain these results. First, even though the inter-trial interval was 5 s, there might have still been some type of memory representation of the target that remained from the preceding movement in FV. Research by Kirsh, Hennighausen and Rösler (2009), found that when individuals performed a movement to a remembered proprioceptive target, they were accurate for up to 8 seconds following the previous movement. However, in considering the limits of our experiment, individuals were performing several trials to and from the target without vision for several seconds. As a result of performing several trials in NV, the initial kinesthetic representation may have become altered. Indeed, our findings coincide with Binsted et al. (2006), who they found that during a reciprocal aiming task, variable error continued to increase even up to 6 s after the targets disappeared. Therefore, it seems as though if individuals can use a proprioceptive representation to execute the subsequent movement, it would have been useful mainly for the first trial in NV. Another explanation could be that individuals were aware of the increase in movement variability, as the trials in NV progressed. As a result of this, individuals may have actively tried to correct their limb trajectory in order to limit movement errors. While it has been stated in previous literature that when individuals actively try to limit error, they commit greater errors in doing so (i.e., the ironic effect; Wegner, Ansfield & Pilloff, 1998), as compared to not actively trying to do so.

<!-- Page 57 -->

48 4.1.4 Conclusion From the research cited in the literature review (see also Study One) it was suggested that when the inter-trial interval is brief (i.e., 2.5 s) individuals rely highly on information from the preceding movement to control the subsequent movement. As a result, endpoint precision of the first trials following a switch in vision condition was reminiscent of the trial that preceded it. In this experiment we increased the inter-trial interval to 5 s to negate the effects of the preceding trial. Indeed, the preceding trial effects observed in the first study were not replicated in this experiment. The distribution of endpoints for the FV trials was always smaller than the NV trials, indicating individuals were more precise when aiming in FV than in NV. Such effect did not change as a function of trial order. In contrast to the first study, effective online visual corrections to the limb trajectory were executed on the first trial that vision was available. Thus, the first trials in NV were not able to benefit from being preceded by a FV trial. Furthermore, the R 2 analysis between movement proportion and movement end indicated there were more amendments made in the FV trials, than NV, suggesting an effective and efficient use of online visual feedback. An additional finding revealed that VE increased as participants performed more than three consecutive trials in NV. Specifically, VE was significantly greater on the 4 th NV trial than on the 1 st NV trial. Furthermore, the R 2 analysis revealed that the 4 th trial in NV also exhibited more trajectory amendments at 25% and 50% of the movement than preceding NV trials. We believe there were several possibilities to explain these findings, which includes - the decaying memory representation of the target location, the use of erroneous proprioceptive feedback, and an ironic effect. In addition, while endpoint precision did not vary across the number of trials in FV, the movement variance analysis revealed low R 2 values for the 4 th trial in FV at 75% of movement. For both results in FV and NV, we do not fully understand why the 4 th trial seems to induce these changes to the movement trajectory; however this may be an indication that there is a change in the control of the movement after certain number of trials (Heath, 2005; Messier & Kalaska, 1999). Altogether, as compared to the offline control hypothesis, which explains the results of the first study, we conclude that; when the inter-trial interval is 5 s, individuals use a largely

<!-- Page 58 -->

49 closed loop mode of control to execute their limb movements. Furthermore, as more trials are performed in a given vision condition the limb trajectory characteristics change, for reasons that will be investigated in future research.

55 General Discussion The present experiments were designed to investigate the strategies individuals use to plan and control their limb movements during a randomized visual feedback schedule. Specifically, we sought to determine if the length of the inter-trial interval mediated different control strategies. In addition, the importance of visual feedback certainty was assessed, by providing information about the vision condition prior to each trial. Generally, the control strategy that has been used to explain human limb control is the closed loop model. At the general level of visual feedback utilization research, it was been found that aiming to a target with the aid of visual feedback is more accurate than when it is not provided (e.g., Carlton, 1992). More specifically, the stochastic submovement model by Meyer et al. (1988) suggested that the number of visual feedback based corrections that are made to the limb depends on the variability of the initial ballistic movement towards the target. Based upon the distance of the limb to the target from the initial ballistic movement, corrective submovements are made to the limb based on visual feedback. As a result if the ballistic movement is significantly off the target, many submovements will be required, while on the other hand if there is very little error then on corrective submovement will suffice. In study one, an open loop mode of limb control was supported, as individuals seemed to use information from the preceding trial to execute the subsequent trials. Specifically, for the first trial following a switch in visual condition (i.e., from NV to FV; FV to NV) the endpoint precision of the trial was the same as the trial that preceded it. As a result, the first NV trial was uncharacteristically precise (i.e., as precise as the FV trials), while the first FV trial was uncharacteristically imprecise. Further support for this explanation was provided by a correlational analysis, which indicated that first NV trial also exhibited the same amount of amendments to the limb as the FV trials. While on the other hand the first FV trial exhibited a stereotyped trajectory, with less movement corrections which is typical of NV trials. To test our secondary objective, we wanted to examine if the reminiscence effects observed in experiment one of the first study were due in part to the uncertainty of a pseudo-randomized visual feedback schedule. As a result, visual feedback certainty was provided in the second experiment, by informing participants of the upcoming vision condition prior to each trial. The results of experiment two revealed similar effects as the first experiment, leading us to believe the adoption

<!-- Page 65 -->

56 of an offline mode of limb control by participants, which were not mediated by the uncertainty of visual feedback under a pseudo-randomized visual feedback schedule. In the second study, which simply employed a longer inter-trial interval (i.e., 5 s) the closed loop perspective was supported, as all movements performed in FV were more precise than those performed in NV. In addition, the analysis of movement variance revealed R 2 values with movement end for the all movements in FV as compared to NV. Taken in combination, these findings suggest that individuals were effectively using visual information to amend their limb trajectories as they were moving towards the target. On the other hand, an intriguing finding was found on the 4 th NV trial: lower R 2 values with movement end were exhibited for the 4 th NV trial as compared to other NV trials. In contrast, endpoint error continually increased as more NV trials were performed. Nevertheless, the proposed explanations still support the closed loop perspective (e.g., individuals were using proprioceptive feedback in an attempt to correct their limb trajectory). Future research should investigate whether providing certainty to individuals during the prolonged inter-trial interval will benefit them. As stated earlier in the worst-case scenario hypothesis (Elliott et al., 2004); individuals may have planned their movements, rather than relying on online control, because they were unsure of the upcoming vision condition. Hence, if visual feedback certainty was provided—by telling the individuals prior to each trial whether vision would be available on the current trial—we would expect variable error in FV to decrease. This result is expected because individuals will be able to better plan and execute online corrections when vision is available. Another possibility for future research can even extend to the area of motor learning research. An interesting and simple question could determine if the inter-trial interval is integral to the process of motor skill acquisition. It has been proposed that practice promotes faster and more efficient use of sensory information (Elliott & Jaeger, 1988). This thesis demonstrated that planning and online control mechanisms are modulated by the inter-trial interval. As such, it is possible that practice scheduling effects (e.g., contextual interference: Shea & Morgan, 1979) require a specific inter-trial interval. Indeed, the beneficial interference between movement motor schema, which is experienced during random practice, clearly arises from the preceding trial. However, should the inter-trial interval be brief for the effect to occur? Is it possible to

<!-- Page 66 -->

57 modulate the effects of contextual interference—or other practice scheduling techniques— simply by manipulating the inter-trial interval? The central contribution of this thesis is that future research in the area of visual feedback use should take into account the importance of the inter-trial interval. As indicated in the first study, a pseudo-randomized visual feedback schedule involving a short inter-trial interval led participants to adopt an offline mode of limb control to direct a manual aiming movement. That is, individuals relied more on visual information from the last than the current trial to execute their manual aiming movement. As a consequence, individuals exhibited uncharacteristically low and high variable error for NV and FV trials, respectively, and that is, if these trials were preceded by a trial in the opposite vision condition. In the second experiment of the first study, we showed that such reliance on visual information from the previous trial was not influenced by advanced information about the upcoming vision condition (i.e., strategy). In contrast, the second study revealed that providing a longer inter-trial interval eliminates the reminiscence effect observed in study one. Such influence of the inter-trial interval may provide an alternate explanation for some classic manual aiming papers. For instance, Elliott and Allard (1985) and Zelaznik et al. (1983) found that when individuals were switched from a blocked to a randomized visual feedback schedule, the differences between FV and NV become less, if at all existent. One problem lies with the fact that the inter-trial interval was not taken into account for these studies. As such, this study offers a clear and novel explanation (cf. strategy: Elliott et al., 2004) for the reduced differences observed between FV and NV in empirical investigations on visual feedback use during goal-directed behaviours.

59 Appendices Appendix A We performed additional analysis of movement variance for experiments 1 and 2 in study 1. The analysis was performed by squaring the correlation coefficients (R 2 ) obtained from correlating the different movement proportions with movement end. From this we subjected the values to an analysis of variance and Tukey HSD post hoc tests with an alpha level of .05. Experiment 1 The ANOVA revealed main effects for vision, F (1, 9) = 5.83, p < .05, movement proportion F (2, 18) = 108, p < .01; and successive trial F (3, 27) = 6.68, p < .01. Also, there were two-way interactions involving vision and movement proportion, F (2, 18) = 10.11, p < .01; and movement proportion with successive trial, F (6,54) = 5.52, p < .01. For the vision by movement proportion interaction, at 25% of the movement there were no differences in R 2 values between FV and NV. However, at 50% and 75% of the movement, NV yielded higher R 2 values than FV. Further, R 2 values increased across all movement proportions for NV but only between 50% and 75% of the movement for FV. For the vision by successive trial interaction, the R 2 value for the second trial in FV was significantly lower than trials in the 2 nd , 3 rd and 4 th trial in NV, while the first trial in NV was significantly lower than the 3 rd and 4 th trial in NV. Lastly, a three-way interaction involving all factors was found F (6,54) = 7.96 p < .01 (see figure 8). Breaking down the interaction revealed no differences between FV and NV at 25% movement proportion, while at 50% movement proportion differences were found between the 2 nd trial in NV and FV. At 75% of movement proportion, the 1 st trial in FV, as it was different from the 1 st trial in NV but not different from the 2 nd , 3 rd and 4 th trial in NV. While the opposite was found for the 1 st trial in NV, as it was different from the 1 st trial in FV but not different from the 2 nd , 3 rd and 4 th in the FV. Also, it is worth noting that R 2 values found for these trials (i.e., 1 st NV trial, 2 nd , 3 rd , 4 th FV trial at 75%) were not different from the 2 nd , 3 rd and 4 th trial in NV at 50% of movement proportion. Experiment 2 The ANOVA revealed main effects for vision, F (1, 11) = 4.99, p < .05, movement proportion F (2, 22) = 129, p < .01; and successive trial F (3, 33) = 10.43, p < .01. Also, there were two-way

<!-- Page 69 -->

60 interactions involving vision and movement proportion, F (2, 22) = 6.96, p < .01; vision and trial, F (3, 33) = 4.32, p < .05. For the vision by movement proportion interaction, at 25% of the movement there were no differences in R 2 values between FV and NV. However, at 75% of the movement, NV yielded higher R 2 values than FV. Further, R 2 values increased across all movement proportions for NV but only between 50% and 75% of the movement for FV. For the vision by successive trial interaction, the R 2 value for the 4 th trial in NV was significantly higher than values found in the 1 st , 2 nd , 3 rd trial in FV as well as the 1 st and 2 nd trial in NV. Lastly, a three-way interaction involving all factors was found F (6, 66) = 12.95, p < .01 (see figure 9). Breaking down the interaction, there were no differences found between NV and FV at 25% movement proportion, while at 50% of the movement differences were found between the 4 th trial FV and NV. At 75% of movement proportion, the 1 st trial in NV was different from the 1 st trial in FV, but not different from the 2 nd , 3 rd and 4 th trial in FV. While the 1 st trial in FV, was different from the 1 st trial in NV but not the 2 nd 3 rd trial in NV. Also, within the NV condition at 75% the 1st trial exhibited the lowest R 2 value before increasing again but stabilizing on the 2 nd and 3 rd trial and finally, significantly increasing on the 4 th trial.
